turn_text: The GMO labeling issue has been through the House of Representatives and the Senate Agriculture Committee spent time talking about the safety of crops that are genetically modified. Do you have a personal view on those crops, Senator, and how big is this labeling proposal that may come before the Senate?

Well, I support biotechnology and it's clear from the science that we're talking about a safe technology. Obviously, if there ever was a concern about it, I'd want to make sure that the right folks were weighing in to make sure it's safe. But everything I've seen from the science is that not only is biotechnology safe, but it's critical for us in terms of feeding a hungry world that is growing every single day. And so we're in a situation now where, because of, unfortunately, There are a lot of confusion around what GE or GMO products really are. And frankly, there's a legitimate growing interest by consumers and only more information about their food and so on and having more choices. We're in a situation where we have, I think, a very difficult situation for farmers for the industry at the same time in meeting concerns of consumers around the country. The idea of having a 50 state patchwork of labeling laws makes no sense. It would be very, very bad for our industry, very bad for the economy. So we've got to take some action that will eliminate a 50 state approach. I think the way to do that, because I believe that our technology is safe, is one in which we create a way to disclose and have transparency. in education about biotechnology, make sure that whatever we do as a national policy doesn't stigmatize biotechnology, but that we come together and find a way to make sure that people have the opportunity to know what's in their food, not just in biotechnology, but other things as well. And I think we could put together a national system of disclosure and transparency that's that user-friendly from the industry standpoint as well as consumers and that there is a way to come up with something that really is a compromise between the two positions. I'm hoping that's possible.
Are electronics a way to resolve that, per se, with a smartphone or the internet? Because, frankly, some food products aren't that big and there's not a lot of room for a label.

Well, I agree that using our new technology, what's called a QR code, we already have the codes on the back of most products here as you're going to check out with the price and so on. I think many, many companies are stepping up with very impressive websites providing a lot of different information that consumers are interested in. And there really is a way to connect those things. And so USDA has also been a very thoughtful way working with folks on how that might be done. So I do believe that there's a way to use technology in a way that gives consumers the information that they need and want and does it in a straightforward way that doesn't stigmatize biotechnology and would cut out this, I think, impossible situation of a 50-state patchwork of labeling laws.

Well, I think it has to be as soon as possible. And I've been also working with those who want to see mandatory labeling to work with them on an approach that would meet the needs of consumers but do it in a way. that is effective and supportive of industry and biotechnology.
